0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter in his corpus opens with a thanksgiving to God for the recipients; Galatians has none. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1531) is the most celebrated commentary in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Catherine von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. He wrote: “I do not know whether I have written anything better about the gospel than my commentary on Galatians.” For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
The letter begins with a defense of apostolic authority and immediately escalates to a declaration that would have shocked its first hearers: the gospel Paul preached is not of human origin, and anyone — even an angel from heaven — who preaches a different gospel is under divine curse. The word translated “accursed” is anathema — the strongest possible language of divine condemnation. Paul uses it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9), the repetition signaling that this is not rhetorical heat but deliberate, settled conviction.

The reason for the severity is simple: if the gospel can be modified by human authority — by apostles, by tradition, by ecclesiastical consensus — then it is not the gospel of God but the gospel of men. And the gospel of men, however sincerely presented, however religiously decorated, cannot save. Only the gospel that comes from God can bring a person into right standing with God. The divine origin of the gospel is therefore not an abstract theological claim; it is the practical ground of the gospel’s saving power.

Paul then makes his case autobiographically. He was not taught the gospel by the Jerusalem apostles; he received it directly from Jesus Christ, by revelation. The account of his conversion and his minimal contact with the Jerusalem church in the years that followed is not self-congratulation but an argument: his gospel is independently and divinely authenticated. It is the same gospel the Jerusalem apostles preach — but its authority does not rest on their endorsement. It rests on the revelation of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Even Paul’s greeting is loaded with theology. He establishes from the first line what the letter will argue: his apostleship is “not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” The Judaizers were apparently questioning his credentials — suggesting that he was a derivative apostle, dependent on Jerusalem for his authority and therefore bound by Jerusalem’s requirements. Paul refuses that framing from the very first word.

The theological summary of the gospel in verses 3–5 is compact and precise: “grace and peace” from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age.” Three things: the giving is voluntary (he gave himself, not was taken), the purpose is substitutionary (for our sins, as our representative and substitute), and the result is deliverance (from the present evil age, the age of sin and bondage into which Adam’s fall plunged humanity). The gospel is grace — and grace flows from the will of the Father (“according to the will of our God and Father”). It was not an emergency measure but the eternal purpose of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as God’s Initiative

The greeting’s theological summary is a miniature of the whole letter: grace, not human effort; Christ’s giving of himself, not our earning of favor; deliverance from the power of the age, not self-improvement within it. Reformed theology has always insisted that salvation originates entirely in God — in his electing grace, his sending of the Son, his application of redemption through the Spirit. Galatians 1:3–5 grounds that conviction in the earliest christological formula: the one who “gave himself for our sins” did so “according to the will of our God and Father.” The cross was the Father’s plan, executed by the Son’s willing self-offering. Grace is not reactive; it is eternal initiative.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatians had received this gospel of grace and had begun to experience its power. Then teachers arrived suggesting that grace alone was insufficient — that circumcision and law-observance were also required. Paul’s opening is a declaration that the gospel they first received was complete. Not a foundation to be built on with religious works, but the whole edifice. Now: Every religious system that adds requirements to grace — sacramental performance, moral achievement, spiritual experience — is doing what the Judaizers did. The gospel is not a starting point to be surpassed; it is the permanent ground on which the entire Christian life stands. Grace from first to last.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle — not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead — and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary: The defense of apostolic authority in the very first phrase is unusual even for Paul — he typically gives his credentials in a subordinate clause, not the letter’s headline. Here it is the headline, because the entire argument about to unfold depends on it: his gospel comes from God, not from any human tradition or ecclesiastical structure. “Not from men nor through man” — two prepositions that distinguish origin (not from men, meaning no human is the source) and mediation (not through man, meaning no human intermediary delivered it). Direct revelation from Jesus Christ: this is the ground of Galatians’ entire theological argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Who gave himself” — the reflexive pronoun is deliberate: not given by others, not taken against his will, but self-offered. The cross was the Son’s free, willing, active self-donation. “For our sins” — substitutionary, on our behalf, in our place. “To deliver us from the present evil age” — the gospel is not merely personal forgiveness but cosmic rescue, a transfer from one realm of existence to another, from the age of sin and death to the age of the Spirit and life. And all of this “according to the will of our God and Father” — grace is not improvisation but eternal purpose. The doxology that closes the greeting (“to whom be the glory”) is the appropriate response to grace: not pride in what we have achieved but praise for what he has given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul omits the customary thanksgiving and goes straight to astonishment and warning. “I am astonished” — the Greek thaumazō can express either wonder at something glorious or bewilderment at something absurd. Here it is the latter: the Galatians are abandoning the gospel for something that is not a gospel at all. And they are doing it “so quickly” — either after a short time as Christians, or rapidly after the Judaizers arrived, or both. The gospel’s grip on the heart is more fragile than we suppose.

The double anathema of verses 8–9 is the most severe language Paul ever uses. An anathema in the Old Testament was something devoted to God for destruction (Lev 27:28–29). To be anathema was to be placed outside the community of the redeemed and under divine judgment. Paul says: whoever preaches a gospel different from the one you received — even if it is Paul himself, even if it is an angel from heaven — is anathema. The authority of the gospel exceeds even the authority of the apostle who proclaimed it. The gospel stands over Paul; Paul does not stand over the gospel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Impossibility of a Better Gospel

Paul’s double anathema reflects the Reformed conviction that the gospel of justification by faith alone is not one theological option among several but the truth of God about salvation, derived from Scripture, non-negotiable and non-improvable. The Reformers did not see themselves as innovating; they saw themselves as recovering. And the recovery was urgent, because what was being lost — in the medieval church’s system of merit, penance, and indulgences — was the same thing being lost in Galatia: the sufficiency of Christ’s atoning work. Luther read Galatians 1:8–9 and recognized himself and his opponents: the Pope and the councils who were preaching a “different gospel” were, in Paul’s terms, anathema. The stakes of the gospel debate are never merely academic.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers were probably sincere. They believed they were adding to the gospel, not replacing it. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance; the law was divinely given. They were not conscious apostates but well-meaning teachers who had fundamentally misunderstood the relationship between law and grace. The road to anathema is paved with sincere intentions. Now: The “different gospel” today rarely presents itself as a different gospel; it presents itself as a more complete or more culturally relevant version of the gospel. Any version that makes human moral performance, spiritual experience, or religious observance part of the ground of justification has crossed Paul’s line. The test is not sincerity of intention but fidelity to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel — not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Deserting him who called you” — the desertion is not merely of a theological position but of the God who called them. To abandon the gospel of grace is to abandon the God of grace — not to find a different version of the same God but to turn away from him entirely, however religious the movement may appear. “There is not another” — the Judaizers’ message was not an alternative gospel; it was a distortion of the one gospel, a counterfeit that bore the name while destroying the substance. The word “distort” (metastrepsai) means to pervert, to reverse, to turn inside out. Adding law to grace does not supplement it; it inverts it.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The double anathema is not heated rhetoric followed by immediate retraction; he repeats it in cold blood (“as we have said before, so now I say again”). The hypothetical cases are deliberately extreme: even Paul himself, even an angel from heaven. The authority of the gospel exceeds any human or angelic messenger, including the messenger who first proclaimed it. This is a crucial epistemological point: the criterion for judging teaching is not the prestige of the teacher but conformity to the apostolic gospel. Paul does not ask the Galatians to trust him; he asks them to weigh what is preached against what was first delivered. The gospel is the judge; the preacher is the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The anathema passages were not the words of a people-pleaser; only a man-pleaser softens the gospel to avoid offense. Paul’s willingness to pronounce anathema on any teacher — including himself — is the evidence of his freedom from human approval. This verse introduces one of the letter’s persistent themes: the gospel liberates from the tyranny of human judgment. The person who must have human approval will always be vulnerable to the Judaizer’s offer — a more socially acceptable, less offensive, less demanding version of Christianity. The servant of Christ trades that approval for something better: the knowledge that he stands in the truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now gives the autobiographical argument for the divine origin of his gospel. The argument has two parts: first, the gospel he received was by direct revelation from Jesus Christ, not derived from human instruction (vv. 11–17); second, his minimal contact with the Jerusalem apostles in the years after his conversion confirms that his gospel was independently received — he did not go to Jerusalem to be trained or commissioned by the Twelve (vv. 18–24). The implication: his gospel stands on its own divine authority.

The account of his conversion is one of the most theologically loaded personal narratives in the New Testament. He was a zealous persecutor of the church — a man who believed he was serving God by destroying the community of those who named Jesus as Messiah. Then God, who “had set him apart before he was born,” “called him by his grace,” and revealed his Son to him. Three words are worth savoring: “set apart” (election — before Paul was born, before he believed, before he persecuted), “called” (effectual grace — the call that creates its own response), “revealed his Son in me” (the gospel is not information received from outside but a revelation of the Son to the inner person by the Spirit). This is the Reformed theology of grace in biographical form.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Calling, and Revelation: The Grammar of Grace

Galatians 1:15–16 is one of the most compact statements of sovereign grace in Paul’s letters. God set Paul apart before birth, called him in grace, and revealed his Son in him. Three divine acts, none of which Paul initiated, earned, or cooperated with in any prior way. His pre-conversion condition — persecutor of the church, zealous for the traditions, a man advancing beyond his peers in Judaism — is the most emphatic possible statement that grace was operative entirely from God’s side. Paul was not seeking God when God found him. He was actively opposing God when grace interrupted him. This is the grammar of grace: God’s sovereign initiative precedes and creates human response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers may have questioned Paul’s authority by pointing to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival in the apostolic circle. He answers: his gospel did not come through the Twelve; it came through Jesus Christ directly. His authority is therefore not derivative but original. Now: Paul’s testimony is the model of every conversion: it is always divine initiative, divine revelation, divine calling that brings a person to Christ. No one comes to the Son unless the Father draws them (John 6:44). The autobiography of every believer, rightly written, has God as its chief actor.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Not man’s gospel” (kata anthrōpon) — not according to a human standard, not of human origin, not subject to human modification. Paul is making the claim that the gospel he preached has a divine pedigree that transcends any human tradition, including the tradition of the Jerusalem church. This is not arrogance; it is the ground of the gospel’s authority. A gospel that derives its authority from human consensus can be revised by human consensus. A gospel that derives its authority from the revelation of Jesus Christ cannot. The Judaizers were, in effect, claiming human apostolic authority for their additional requirements; Paul denies that any human authority can override the revealed gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s pre-conversion curriculum vitae is offered as evidence against any suggestion that his gospel is softened Judaism. He was not a lapsed Jew seeking a more gracious alternative; he was an exemplary Jew — advancing beyond his peers, zealous for the ancestral traditions, so convinced of his religious duty that he persecuted and tried to destroy the very community he would soon lead. The word “violently” (hyperbolen) — in Greek it means “beyond measure.” This was not casual observance; it was passionate, all-consuming religious devotion. Which makes the reversal all the more dramatic: the zealot became the apostle. That kind of reversal requires divine intervention, not human education.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone; nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Set me apart before I was born” — the language echoes Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1, prophets who were called before birth for a specific mission. Paul is claiming the same prophetic pattern: God’s purpose for him predates his existence. The call came through grace, not through merit. And the revelation was of the Son — not information about the Son but the Son himself, revealed to and in Paul (“in me,” en emoi). The gospel is not merely intellectual content; it is the living reality of the risen Christ making himself known. After this, Paul did not go to Jerusalem. He went to Arabia — perhaps to the wilderness, to pray and be taught by the Spirit in solitude. His gospel needed no human certification.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother. (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary: Three years passed between Paul’s conversion and his first visit to Jerusalem — and that visit was brief, fifteen days, with only Peter and James. This is Paul’s point: if his gospel had been derived from the Jerusalem apostles, you would expect intensive consultation, extended training, formal commissioning. Instead: three years of independent ministry, then a brief visit. The parenthetical oath — “before God, I do not lie!” — signals that he knows his account strains credulity. But it is precisely the implausibility of the timeline that makes his argument: his gospel did not come through Jerusalem; it came through revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary: The churches of Judea did not know Paul by face — only by reputation. And the reputation was a wonder: the persecutor had become the preacher. “They glorified God because of me” — not because of Paul’s brilliance or theological training but because of what God had done. The reversal of the persecutor is the most visible demonstration that the gospel is the power of God, not the product of human education. Paul’s testimony was itself a piece of the gospel it proclaimed: divine grace, sovereign and transforming, operating on the most unlikely of subjects. The doxology of the Judean churches is the appropriate response to every genuine conversion.

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Fourteen years after his conversion — and apparently prompted by a divine revelation — Paul went up to Jerusalem and laid before the apostles the gospel he had been preaching among the Gentiles. The meeting was private, with the leaders, to ensure that his mission had not been “running in vain.” This is not uncertainty about the truth of his gospel; it is pastoral wisdom about the unity of the church. A gospel affirmed by the Jerusalem leaders and a gospel practiced in Antioch must be the same gospel if the church is to be one.

The test case was Titus: a Greek, uncircumcised, present at the Jerusalem meeting. If the Jerusalem leaders required his circumcision, the Judaizers’ position would be vindicated. They did not require it. The “false brothers” (probably the Judaizers themselves or their allies) had slipped in to spy on the “freedom we have in Christ Jesus,” but Paul refused to yield “even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.” This is the pastoral reason for theological firmness: the truth of the gospel must be guarded for the sake of the congregations who depend on it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel Unity and the Circumcision Question

The Jerusalem conference established a principle of first importance: the same gospel applies to Jews and Gentiles without differentiation at the point of justification. Both are justified by faith alone, not by circumcision or any covenant marker. This is not a sociological or cultural inclusivity statement; it is a theological claim about the nature of justification. The covenant of grace in Christ is entered by faith, and faith alone, by every member of humanity regardless of ethnic or religious background. The Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Savior, one way of entry — finds its clearest New Testament expression in the Jerusalem conference’s verdict on Titus.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatian congregations were being told that Gentile Christians needed to add circumcision to their faith. Paul says: I took exactly this question to Jerusalem, and the apostles affirmed that circumcision was not required. The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them. Now: The principle at stake — that no ethnic, religious, or cultural marker supplements faith as the ground of acceptance with God — applies wherever the church is tempted to create a two-tier Christianity: fully accepted Christians who have satisfied some additional requirement, and Christians who have “only” faith. There is no such two-tier. Faith in Christ is the only criterion, for all people, in every culture, in every generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourteen years of independent gospel ministry before a second Jerusalem visit is Paul’s argument in numbers: his gospel did not need Jerusalem’s approval to operate powerfully and authentically. He went, prompted by divine revelation, not by summons or need for validation. “Those who seemed influential” — the Greek phrase (tois dokousin) is slightly ironic, not dismissive of the apostles’ genuine authority but refusing to ground authority in human reputation rather than divine appointment. The private meeting before the public assembly was pastoral wisdom, not theological timidity.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in — who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery — to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Titus was the test case, and he passed: the Jerusalem leaders did not require his circumcision. Then came the “false brothers” — people who were inside the community but outside the gospel, whose agenda was to surveil and subvert the freedom of grace. Paul names what they were after with precision: “to bring us into slavery.” The Judaizers’ gospel was not a richer version of freedom; it was bondage dressed in religious clothing. And Paul’s response was total and immediate: “not even for a moment.” Gospel compromise is not gradual; it begins the moment you yield the first inch. He yielded nothing, “so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you” — the pastoral reason for theological firmness. Your freedom depends on the truth being kept.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality) — those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked through me also for mine to the Gentiles), and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, when they recognized the grace that was given to me, they agreed that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Added nothing to me” — the verdict of the Jerusalem conference on Paul’s gospel: nothing lacking, nothing to supplement, nothing to correct. The handshake of fellowship (the “right hand of fellowship”) between Paul and Barnabas on one side and James, Peter, and John on the other is one of the great moments of apostolic unity: two streams of the one mission, to Gentiles and to Jews, operating under the same gospel with mutual recognition. The only addition was a request Paul was already eager to fulfill: remember the poor. Not a theological addition to the gospel but a practical expression of its social implications — the gospel creates a community that crosses class lines and cares for the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Antioch confrontation is one of the most bracing episodes in the New Testament: Paul publicly rebukes Peter, the acknowledged leader of the Twelve and the first to receive Gentiles into the church (Acts 10). The occasion was table fellowship — specifically, whether Jewish and Gentile Christians could eat together. Peter had been eating with Gentiles (a significant social-religious act in that culture) until “certain people from James” arrived from Jerusalem, at which point he withdrew and separated himself, “fearing the circumcision party.”

Paul’s analysis of what Peter was doing is devastating: “he stood condemned.” The issue was not dietary preference or social convention; it was whether the gospel’s logic was being lived. If Peter could eat with Gentiles when no Jewish observers were present but withdrew when they arrived, he was effectively teaching by behavior that Gentile Christians were second-class members of the covenant community — acceptable at table when it was socially safe, but expendable when social cost demanded. That behavior “was not in step with the truth of the gospel.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Must Govern Behavior, Not Just Belief

Paul’s confrontation with Peter illustrates a principle the Reformers would later articulate as semper reformanda: the church is always to be reformed according to the gospel, which means the gospel must govern not only doctrinal statements but social practices, power dynamics, and table habits. Peter believed the right doctrine — he had proclaimed the equality of Jews and Gentiles before God (Acts 10–11). But his behavior contradicted that belief under social pressure. This is the nature of hypocrisy in Paul’s sense: not the cynical pretense of faith one does not hold, but the failure to live consistently with faith one genuinely holds. The gospel demands not merely assent but integration.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter’s withdrawal from table fellowship with Gentiles was not theologically motivated; it was socially motivated. He feared the circumcision party. Fear of human judgment — the same snare Paul identified in 1:10 (“am I trying to please man?”) — was the mechanism of his compromise. Now: The church is always tempted to practice a gospel in comfortable company that it abandons when social cost arrives. The test of whether we believe the gospel is not what we confess in church but how we behave when the confession is costly. Do we treat brothers and sisters of different backgrounds, classes, or cultures as equally and fully members of the one body — not when it is easy but when it is expensive?

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain people came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I opposed him to his face” — not in a private memo, not through diplomatic intermediaries, but face to face, publicly. The stakes were too high for courtesy to override clarity. Peter was “condemned” (kategnōsmenos) — the verb is a judicial term: found guilty, standing self-condemned by the contradiction between his belief and his behavior. The cause of the condemnation was fear: he was “fearing the circumcision party.” This is the same fear that drove the Galatians to consider adding circumcision to the gospel: the fear of human judgment, the need for approval from those who represent the religious establishment. Fear of man is always the mechanism of gospel compromise.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary: Hypocrisy here means acting in a way inconsistent with what you believe — playing a role (hypokrisis) that your convictions do not support. Even Barnabas, Paul’s trusted partner, was swept along. The social pressure was overwhelming; Peter’s example was authoritative. Only Paul, who had learned the hard way that the fear of man makes the gospel impossible, stood firm. His public rebuke to Peter exposes the practical contradiction: Peter had been living as a Gentile (eating with them), which means he knew that Jewish food laws were not binding in Christ. Now, by withdrawing, he was implying that Gentiles needed to “live like Jews.” You cannot live one way and require another. The gospel must be consistent or it is not the gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Whether verses 15–21 are still Paul’s speech to Peter or have become a direct address to the Galatians is disputed, but the theological content is the letter’s defining statement. The argument moves with precision: we (Jewish Christians, who already know that the law cannot justify) have believed in Christ in order to be justified by faith, because no one is justified by works of the law. If even we Jews needed to come to Christ for justification, how much more do Gentiles? And if seeking to be justified by Christ alone is consistent with righteousness, then there is no failure of the gospel in the absence of circumcision.

The great verse is 2:20, which is not merely a beautiful personal testimony but a theological claim of the first order. “I have been crucified with Christ” — Paul’s personal death in Christ’s death, his old self — the self defined by performance, by law-keeping, by seeking justification through human effort — is finished, crucified, done. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” — the replacement self is not an improved Paul but an indwelling Christ, who is the source, content, and character of Paul’s new existence. “The Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” — the universal gospel comes to personal address: not merely “for the world” but for me, individually, by name.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Luther called justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae — the article by which the church stands or falls. Galatians 2:15–21 is the locus classicus for this doctrine. Justification is forensic (a legal declaration, not a moral transformation, though transformation follows); it is by faith alone (sola fide); its object is Christ alone (solus Christus); and it is by grace alone (sola gratia). The Reformed tradition has always insisted that these three “alones” stand or fall together: take away any one and you have taken away all three. If faith is not the exclusive instrument of justification, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of that faith, it is not grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish Christians had the most sophisticated religious background imaginable — the law, the covenant, the Temple, the sacrificial system. And Paul says: even we found that the law could not justify us, which is why we came to Christ. The argument from Jewish to Gentile Christian is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those for whom it was given, it certainly cannot justify those who received it only secondarily. Now: The person who comes to faith after a life of moral respectability and the person who comes to faith from a life of obvious failure stand in exactly the same position before God: both are justified by faith alone, both have the same righteousness (Christ’s), both stand on the same ground. The moral respectability is as irrelevant to justification as the moral failure. Only faith in Christ counts.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Works of the law” (erga nomou) refers to the deeds required by the Mosaic law, particularly the covenant markers that distinguished Israel from the nations (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath). More broadly, it encompasses all human religious performance offered as the ground of divine acceptance. The verdict is unambiguous: no one will be justified by such works. Not because the law is defective but because human performance of it is always defective — and because the law was never designed to justify but to expose sin and point to the Justifier. “Faith in Jesus Christ” is the alternative — not faith as a work that earns justification, but faith as the hand that receives the righteousness Christ has earned.

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary: An objection anticipated: if justification by faith means that the law’s requirements no longer determine one’s standing, and if Jewish Christians are now found eating with Gentiles (like Peter before he withdrew) in apparent violation of the law, does that make Christ a promoter of lawlessness? Paul’s answer is mē genoito — the strongest possible Greek negative, “certainly not,” “by no means,” “God forbid.” The freedom of the gospel is not lawlessness; it is the fulfillment of the law’s intent through love (5:14). Christ does not promote sin; he destroys sin’s power over those who belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “If I rebuild what I tore down” — the thing Paul tore down when he came to faith was his attempt to establish righteousness through law-keeping. If he now rebuilds that system — if he re-erects the structure of performance-based acceptance — he proves that he was wrong to tear it down, and therefore that his original transgression (seeking righteousness through law rather than through Christ) was the truth after all. But the law itself accomplished his death to the law: by revealing sin in its fullness (Rom 7:7–11), the law drove him to the end of himself and to Christ. “I died to the law, so that I might live to God” — death to the law as a system of self-justification is the precondition of life to God in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I have been crucified with Christ” — the perfect tense in Greek indicates a past event with permanent present results. Paul’s old self — the self defined by performance and self-justification — died in Christ’s death. Not metaphorically but really, by virtue of union with Christ: what happened to Christ happened to his representative people. The new existence is defined by indwelling: “Christ who lives in me.” And the life of this new existence is “by faith in the Son of God” — not occasional dependence on Christ but the constant orientation of life toward him. Then come the most personal words in the letter: “who loved me and gave himself for me.” The gospel that spans the cosmos narrows to a single name. He loved you. He gave himself for you. Personally. The universal act of the cross has a personal address: you. The conclusion is inexorable: if there were any other way to be righteous, Christ died for nothing. There is no other way. His death was the way, the only way, the final way.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with one of the most rhetorical openings in his letters: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” The emotional intensity is pastoral urgency, not contempt. They had received a clear presentation of Christ crucified — Paul describes his preaching as a public placard of the crucifixion (“publicly portrayed as crucified”) — and they had experienced the Spirit in power. Now they are considering adding circumcision and law-observance to the faith they exercised when they received all of this. The absurdity is acute.

The six questions of verses 1–5 are not rhetorical flourishes but a logical argument: everything you received as Christians came through faith, not through law. The Spirit came by faith. The miracles were experienced by faith. If the beginning of your life in Christ was by faith, why would the continuation of it be by law? “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” — the flesh here does not mean sinful desires but human religious effort, circumcision as a fleshly mark, the whole system of law-observance as a human contribution to what the Spirit has begun.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Received by Faith

The argument from the Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit is not an appeal to subjectivism; it is an appeal to the epistemologically significant fact of how the Spirit came to them. The Spirit comes through the proclamation of the gospel received by faith — not through the performance of law-works. This is the experiential confirmation of the theological argument: the mechanism by which God gives the Spirit to his people is faith, not law. Reformed theology has consistently held that the Spirit applies the benefits of Christ to those who believe — the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ, and union with Christ is by faith. Law-works have no role in this transaction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatians had undeniable experiential evidence that the Spirit came through faith: their conversions were accompanied by power, miracles, and obvious transformation. Paul asks them to think: did that happen when you did works of the law, or when you heard and believed the gospel? The question answers itself. Now: The testimony of every genuine conversion is the same: the Spirit came through hearing the gospel with faith. No one receives the Spirit through religious performance; performance cannot open the channel that only faith can open. The ongoing question for the believer is whether they seek the Spirit’s power by continuing in faith or by adding religious effort.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified. Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary: “Bewitched” (ebaskanēn) — the image is of a malign spell cast by someone’s evil eye, drawing a person away from clear thinking. Paul cannot account for the Galatians’ movement toward the Judaizers’ gospel except as a kind of spiritual enchantment. Christ crucified had been “publicly portrayed” before them — the Greek suggests a public announcement placard, the kind used in the ancient world to display official proclamations. The cross was the content of Paul’s preaching, presented with clarity and power. How can anyone who has genuinely seen that cross then turn to law-keeping as the ground of their acceptance? The question about the Spirit is decisive: they know how they received it. And it was not by circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain — if indeed it was in vain? Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary: “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” — this is the logic of the Galatian error exposed. They did not begin their Christian life by doing works of the law; they began it by receiving the Spirit through faith. Now the Judaizers are suggesting that they must advance beyond that beginning by adding law-performance. Paul says: this is regression, not progression. Moving from Spirit to flesh, from faith to works, from grace to performance is not spiritual maturity; it is spiritual foolishness. The miracles they had experienced — happening not through law-keeping but through faith-proclamation — were the evidence standing against the Judaizers’ position.

verseByVerse.quote: just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”. Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: The appeal to Abraham is the cornerstone of Paul’s theological argument. The Judaizers were claiming to represent the Abrahamic tradition. Paul shows that Abraham himself was justified by faith, not by circumcision (he was justified in Genesis 15, four chapters before the circumcision ordinance of Genesis 17). The true sons of Abraham are therefore defined not by circumcision but by the faith Abraham exercised. And the Abrahamic promise was always universal: “in you shall all the nations be blessed.” The gospel Paul was preaching to Gentiles was not a departure from the Abrahamic covenant; it was its fulfillment. Abraham’s blessing was always destined for the nations, always received by faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established that Abraham was justified by faith, Paul now establishes the negative counterpart: those who rely on the law are under a curse. The law itself says, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Deut 27:26). The law demands comprehensive, perfect, continuous obedience. No one achieves this. Therefore, the law can only produce a curse for those who rely on it as the ground of their standing with God.

Then comes the magnificent exchange of verse 13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. He took the curse that the law pronounces on every lawbreaker — and every person who has ever lived under the law is a lawbreaker — onto himself. He “became a curse” by being “hanged on a tree,” fulfilling the pronouncement of Deuteronomy 21:23 that anyone hanged on a tree is cursed. The cross was not merely the site of his death; it was the legal mechanism by which the law’s curse was transferred to him and removed from all who belong to him. This is substitutionary atonement in its most precise legal form.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Logic of the Curse Exchange

The doctrine of penal substitution — that Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, satisfying the law’s demands and exhausting its curse — is not a later theological development but the explicit content of Galatians 3:13. The exchange is legally precise: the curse that the law pronounces on lawbreakers fell on Christ on the cross, so that the blessing the law promises to the perfectly obedient could be given to all who are in Christ. This is not merely sympathetic solidarity (“he suffered with us”) but legal substitution (“he suffered instead of us, in our place, bearing our curse”). The Reformation’s insistence on penal substitution as the heart of the atonement is exegetically grounded here.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers were offering the Galatians the law as a supplementary means of securing divine blessing. Paul shows them that the law, far from delivering blessing, pronounces a curse on all who rely on it — because perfect compliance is the only condition the law accepts, and no one achieves it. The only exit from the law’s curse is the one who became a curse for us. Now: Every person who has ever tried to commend themselves to God by their moral performance has placed themselves under the law’s verdict: “cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things.” There is no partial credit. The law is binary: perfect obedience or curse. Only Christ met the first standard, and only Christ can absorb the second. Faith in him is the only exit.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.” Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The law’s demand is comprehensive: “all things,” “abide by,” “do them.” There is no partial compliance; the law is a unity (James 2:10: “whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it”). To rely on the law as the ground of one’s standing with God is to submit oneself to this comprehensive demand — and to guarantee the curse, because no one meets it. Then Habakkuk 2:4: “the righteous shall live by faith.” Faith and law-reliance are mutually exclusive as the ground of justification. The righteous one lives by faith — trust in God’s promise, not achievement of God’s demand.

verseByVerse.quote: But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.” Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” — so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” This is the theological apex of the chapter. The law and faith operate on different principles: the law says “do and live,” faith says “trust and receive.” Christ bridged the gap not by making the law’s demands easier but by meeting them perfectly on our behalf — and then absorbing the curse that our failure deserved. Deuteronomy 21:23 (“cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”) was fulfilled at Calvary: the cross was the place of the curse, and Christ bore it. The result: the Abrahamic blessing (justification, the Spirit, adoption) flows to the Gentiles through Christ. The curse absorbed; the blessing released; the Spirit given. All through faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now makes a legal-historical argument: a covenant, once ratified, cannot be modified by a later party. God ratified the covenant with Abraham — sealed it with a divine oath (Gen 15, 22) — and promised that the blessing would come through Abraham’s “offspring.” Paul makes the significant exegetical point that “offspring” is singular (“seed,” sperma), not plural, and argues that the singular points to Christ as the singular recipient of the Abrahamic promise. The Mosaic law, which came 430 years later, cannot annul this promise. It operates within a different register. The inheritance promised to Abraham is still received through faith in the promised Offspring, not through law-keeping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to and independent of the Mosaic law. This is one of the most important principles in Reformed covenant theology: the Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant but operates within it, serving it, without modifying its fundamental character as a covenant of promise received by faith. The Abrahamic promise was not conditioned on Mosaic law-observance; it was conditioned on the faithfulness of the Seed, who is Christ. The inheritance is therefore still received by those who share Abraham’s faith, in the same Seed Abraham believed in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers were effectively arguing that the Mosaic law, given later, modified the conditions of the Abrahamic covenant. Paul shows this is legally impossible: a ratified covenant cannot be revoked or amended by a later addition. The law did not create a new way to receive the promise; it served the promise until the promised Seed arrived. Now: The argument that religious observance improves on or supplements the Abrahamic-covenant basis of salvation is as old as the Galatian crisis. Every generation needs to hear: the promise came first; the promise is in Christ; the promise is received by faith. Nothing adds to it.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The legal analogy is simple: a ratified will or covenant cannot be voided or amended by a subsequent party. God’s covenant with Abraham, once sworn and sealed, stands. Then the exegetical observation: “offspring” (sperma) is singular. This is not fanciful wordplay; Paul is drawing on an important feature of the Abrahamic promise — that the blessing would come through one particular heir, the Seed of the woman (Gen 3:15), the seed of Abraham, the son of David. The singular is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the one Offspring who inherits all that God promised to Abraham and through whom all the nations receive the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chronological argument is decisive: 430 years separate the Abrahamic covenant from the giving of the Mosaic law. The law came after the promise, within the promise, in service of the promise — but it cannot supersede or modify a promise already unconditionally sealed by God. The two operate on fundamentally different principles: promise is unconditional and received by faith; law is conditional and demands performance. If the inheritance had come by law, it would no longer be a promise; if by promise, law-keeping cannot be its condition. God chose the promise; the law serves that choice without replacing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify and cannot nullify the promise, what is it for? Paul’s answer is precise and multi-layered. The law was “added because of transgressions” — to make sin explicit, to reveal its nature, to expose the depth of the problem that only the gospel can solve. It was “until the offspring should come” — temporary, purposeful, designed for a specific period in redemptive history. It was “put in place through angels by an intermediary” (Moses) — whereas the Abrahamic promise came directly from God, indicating the law’s subordinate status.

The metaphor of the guardian (paidagōgos) in verse 24 is the chapter’s most vivid image. A paidagōgos in the ancient world was a household slave entrusted with the oversight of a child — accompanying him to school, supervising his behavior, keeping him safe and disciplined. The slave was not the teacher; he got the child to the teacher. The law was Israel’s paidagōgos — not the source of life or justification, but the severe and necessary guardian that walked the nation through its childhood until Christ, the Teacher, arrived. Now that Christ has come, the guardian’s function has been completed: “we are no longer under a guardian.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Temporary, Purposeful, Fulfilled

Reformed covenant theology has always insisted on the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while acknowledging the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within redemptive history. The law’s role as guardian is an example of this: it was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a specific phase, not the final phase. Its abolition as a system of justification is not God changing his mind but God completing his plan. The law pointed to Christ; Christ has come; the finger can now rest.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers wanted to reinstall the guardian after the child had come of age. Paul says: the guardian was dismissed by divine design. To return to it is to misunderstand both the law and the gospel. Now: The Christian who tries to use the law as the ground of their standing before God is acting like a child who insists on being escorted to school after they have already graduated. The guardian served its purpose. Christ has come. Faith in him is the direct relationship for which the law was always preparing the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary. Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Added because of transgressions” — the law was added to make transgressions explicit, to give sin its legal character as rebellion against God’s known command (Rom 5:13: “sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law”). The law revealed the depth of the problem: Israel’s history under the law is a record of repeated transgression against a clearly known standard. This revelation of sin was a gift, not a condemnation — it drove the nation toward the need for the Promised Seed. The mediation through angels and Moses signals the law’s subordinate status; the Abrahamic promise came directly from the one God.

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary: The law and the promise are not opposed; they serve the same purpose but in different modes. The law cannot give life — it was never designed to; its function is diagnostic, not curative. “The Scripture imprisoned everything under sin” — not arbitrarily but redemptively, so that there would be no other door, no alternative exit, no competing source of the righteousness that only the promise in Christ can provide. The imprisonment is grace: it closes every avenue of self-justification so that the only open door is faith in Jesus Christ. The law’s severity is the negative image of the gospel’s generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Before faith came” — Paul speaks of “faith” (pistis) both as a subjective act and as an objective era: the era of the new covenant, the age of the Spirit in which justifying faith is openly and fully available through the proclaimed gospel of Christ. The law held God’s people in a kind of protective custody during this period of waiting — kept them from total dissolution, kept sin’s nature visible, kept the need for a Savior urgent. Now the Savior has come. The guardian is dismissed. “We are no longer under a guardian” — this is not antinomianism (the law’s moral demands are fulfilled by those who walk in the Spirit, 5:14, 16), but it is the end of the law as the defining framework of the covenant relationship. That framework is now Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter concludes with one of the most revolutionary social-theological statements in the New Testament. In Christ Jesus, through faith, all who believe are “sons of God” — mature heirs of the promise, no longer minors under a guardian. The baptismal formula of verse 27 (“as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ”) grounds this new status in union with Christ: to be baptized into Christ is to be clothed in him, enveloped in his identity, defined by his status rather than one’s own.

Then comes the great statement of verse 28: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This is not the erasure of difference but the establishment of a unity that transcends every humanly significant difference. Ethnicity, social status, and gender — the three primary categories by which ancient society (and most of human history) stratifies people — are all rendered irrelevant at the point of standing before God and membership in the covenant community. All are one in Christ. All are equally heirs of Abraham’s promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel and Human Dignity: Unity in Christ

Galatians 3:28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals; it creates a new community in which the stratifications of the old age are overcome by the unity of the new. Reformed theology has always insisted that this is not merely idealism but eschatological reality: those who are in Christ are already, now, equally members of the covenant people, equally heirs of the promise, equally clothed in Christ’s righteousness. The social implications of justification by faith are total: if everyone stands before God on exactly the same ground (the righteousness of Christ received by faith), then no one has any basis for regarding another as inferior in the community of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In the first century, the Jew/Gentile, slave/free, male/female distinctions were not merely social categories; they were legally, religiously, and socially determinative of one’s status in every institution, including the synagogue. The Galatian churches were being told by the Judaizers that Gentile believers were second-class members. Paul says: in Christ, that category is abolished. Now: The church always faces pressure to re-introduce some version of these distinctions — whether of race, class, gender, education, or social background. Galatians 3:28 is the permanent rebuke: in Christ there is one body, one Spirit, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father. The diversity is real and good; the unity is foundational and non-negotiable.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Sons of God” — not children-under-guardians, not minors awaiting their inheritance, but sons in the fullest sense: heirs, mature members of the household, with direct access to the Father. This status is through faith — and it is confirmed and expressed in baptism, understood here as the rite of entry into union with Christ. “Put on Christ” is a vivid metaphor: to be clothed in Christ, to have his identity become yours, his righteousness covering your sin, his status before the Father defining your status. When God looks at the baptized believer, he sees them dressed in his Son. The Father’s response to that sight is the same as his response to his Son: “This is my beloved child, in whom I am well pleased.”

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary: The three pairs — Jew/Greek (ethnicity), slave/free (social class), male/female (gender) — were the primary axes of stratification in the ancient world. Paul declares each pair irrelevant at the point of union with Christ and membership in his body. This is not the obliteration of difference but the subordination of every human difference to the one decisive identity: being in Christ. And the practical conclusion: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.” Gentiles who believe are not second-class members of a primarily Jewish covenant; they are full heirs of the promise made to Abraham, co-heirs with Christ of everything God promised. The promise always aimed at this: a multinational, multi-ethnic, economically diverse family of faith, all one in the one Seed.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane, now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “I am in the anguish of childbirth again until Christ is formed in you.” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s legal analogy is drawn from everyday Roman and Greek inheritance law: a minor heir, however wealthy his father’s estate, is for all practical purposes indistinguishable from a slave — subject to guardians and managers, unable to act on his own authority, waiting for the date set by the father. This was Israel’s condition under the law — heirs of the promise but living under custodians, in the “childhood” of redemptive history, awaiting the Father’s appointed time.

Then “the fullness of time” arrived, and God sent two gifts: first, his Son, born into the conditions of the problem (born of woman, born under the law) in order to solve it from within (to redeem those under the law); second, the Spirit of his Son, sent into our hearts, producing the cry “Abba! Father!” The double sending — of Son and Spirit — is the shape of the gospel. The Son accomplishes redemption and adoption; the Spirit applies it, seals it, and causes the heart to experience it as real. The result is not improved servitude but transformed status: “you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Galatians 4:4–6 is one of the most trinitarian passages in Paul’s letters. God the Father sends the Son; the Father (and Son) sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions — what Reformed theology calls the missio Dei — are coordinated and inseparable: the external mission of the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities; the internal mission of the Spirit applies those realities to the heart, causing the adopted child to know and cry out to the Father. The theology of adoption (huiothesia) has its clearest statement here: we are not merely forgiven (though we are); we are brought into the family, given the status of sons, welcomed into the intimacy of the Father’s house. John Stott writes that adoption is “the highest privilege the gospel offers.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatians had been adopted as sons — they had the Spirit, they had cried “Abba,” they had known the freedom of the Father’s house. Now they were considering a return to the slave’s existence, performing works to earn what they already possessed as a gift. The absurdity is acute: the son who has been brought into the family does not need to earn his way back in. He is in. Now: The Christian who relates to God primarily through performance — who prays with one eye on whether they have done enough to deserve a hearing, who gives in order to feel acceptable, who worships to discharge a religious duty — is living as a slave in the Father’s house. The Spirit of adoption was given to produce the cry “Abba,” not the calculation “what must I do?” The difference is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father. In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: The analogy is precise: the child-heir owns the estate but cannot exercise ownership. He is functionally a slave to those who manage what is already his. Paul applies this to humanity (both Jew and Gentile) under the “elementary principles of the world” (stoicheia tou kosmou) — a phrase that refers to the basic ordering elements of the old age, the rudimentary spiritual and religious structures that governed human life before Christ. For Israel, this included the Mosaic law in its custodial function. For Gentiles, it included the elemental religious observances that bound them to the creation order rather than the Creator. Both were forms of immaturity, awaiting the Father’s appointed time.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The fullness of time” (to plērōma tou chronou) — not an accident of history but the Father’s appointed moment, the date set by the Father (v. 2), the climax of a redemptive history that had been moving toward this point since Eden. The Son did not arrive in spite of the human condition but into it: “born of woman” (fully human, entering our nature), “born under the law” (entering the specific legal situation of those he came to redeem). He came from within the problem to solve it from within. “Redeem” (exagorasē) — to buy out from the market, to ransom; the same word used in 3:13 of redemption from the law’s curse. The goal: “adoption as sons” (huiothesian) — not merely forgiveness but full family membership, the legal status of a son with all the rights and inheritance of sonship.

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The Spirit of his Son” — the Spirit is specifically identified as the Spirit of the Son, the one who conforms believers to the Son and brings them into the Son’s own relationship with the Father. “Abba! Father!” — the Aramaic Abba is Jesus’ own word for the Father in prayer (Mark 14:36; Rom 8:15), the most intimate address available in his culture, something like “dear Father” or “my own Father.” The Spirit places this word on the lips of every adopted child of God — the same word the eternal Son uses in his own communion with the Father. This is not metaphor; it is the most astonishing claim about the Christian’s standing: you address God with the word the Son uses. You are that close. You are that welcome. The status: “no longer a slave, but a son” — and therefore “an heir through God,” an heir not by achievement but by the Father’s own action.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theological argument to personal appeal, and the register shifts dramatically. He reminds the Galatians of what they were before the gospel arrived: slaves to “those that by nature are not gods,” bound to the elemental principles of an age that is passing away. They have been set free. How is it possible, then, that they are “turning back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles”? The Judaizers’ requirements — observing days, months, seasons, years — are, in Paul’s shocking analysis, the same kind of bondage as the pagan religious calendar they left behind. Both are forms of slavery to the elements of the old age.

Then the personal memory: Paul had come to them sick, in bodily weakness, and they had received him “as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.” They would have gouged out their own eyes and given them to him. What happened to that love? The honest pastoral question: “Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?” And the anguish of a spiritual parent: “I am in the anguish of childbirth again until Christ is formed in you.” The purpose of all ministry is not allegiance to the minister but Christ formed in the congregation. Paul is willing to be found the enemy if Christ is found in them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage

Paul’s equation of Judaizing requirements with Gentile pagan observances is one of the most startling moves in the letter. He does not say the law is as bad as idol-worship; he says that returning to law-keeping as the ground of one’s standing with God, after having been freed by Christ, is structurally equivalent to the bondage from which the Gentiles came. Both are forms of enslavement to the elements of the old age rather than freedom in Christ. Reformed theology has always insisted that moralism — the attempt to establish one’s standing with God through religious performance, however biblically decorated — is not a minor error but a fundamental misunderstanding of the gospel that produces its own form of spiritual bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatians had known genuine love for Paul and the gospel he preached.
